So, the next thing we're trying to do with the new campaign structure is consolidate as much as possible. And that applies to both campaigns and adsets. We're going to try and run as few campaigns and as few adsets as possible. Often just using the one campaign and the one adset. I'll explain later on when we do and don't want to uh to do that. Why are we doing that? Well, it's best to combine the data into as few elements as possible. Let's say you generate 70 conversions in a week. Instead of having that spread across 10 different adsets, so seven conversions roughly per adset per week, Meta is going to struggle to optimize those adsets. Going to struggle to get out of the learning phase. Whereas, if that's in one adset, you're generating 70 conversions per week in that one adset. Meta is able to fully optimize. They're able to work out the best time of day to advertise, what ad impression frequency is required, advertise to this person instead of this person, use this ad instead of this ad. all the various points that Meta's system optimizes to get us more of what we want, more sales, more leads, whatever it is we've set up our campaign to optimize for, Meta can do that better with more conversion data. So much better to have that consolidated data into the one campaign, one adset as opposed to spread across lots of different elements that will struggle uh to optimize. Second reason why we want to consolidate is because we want to avoid auction overlap. Now, there's some misconceptions around overlap. A lot of people think I'm talking about audience overlap. When I say auction overlap, I'm not audience overlap would be you've got two different campaigns, two different adsets, and they're targeting a lot of the same audience. Now, that's not ideal, but the whole idea of that's going to increase the cost because you're bidding against yourself is a bit silly. There are thousands of advertisers trying to reach the same people. One extra campaign ad setting that not going to make much difference. But you can run into issues with auction overlap, which is a different thing. Meta systems are now very sophisticated at working out what ad impression frequency is required to get the outcome that you want. So Meta might work out, you know what, we're better off at generating four or five ad impressions for a single individual over a 24 48 hour time period as opposed to spreading out those ad impressions over a week. Well, Meta could plan that really well if it's just got the one campaign, one adset targeting a person, a group of people obviously, but we're talking about one individual user in this case, but targeting um a group of people. If you've got some ad impressions coming from one adset, some ad impressions coming from another adset or different campaigns, much more difficult for Meta to work out that delivery system of right, let's put an ad in front of this person four times over the next 48 hours. Much more difficult for them to be able to uh to do that. So, that's that's the issue that comes up with auction overlap. and you want to take advantage of what Meta's delivery system um is able to do. Okay. - The 4-Stage Creative Lifecycle from Static Image to Dedicated Lander: Kind: captions Language: en Everyone talks about a hook. Your hook is everything. You have 3 seconds to stop the scroll. The first frame determines everything. And yes, I'm not going to lie, the hook matters. But here's what nobody talks about. What happens after you find a hook that works? Because finding a winning hook is not the end of the creative process. It's a beginning. A winning hook is just a signal. It tells you that this angle resonate with this audience. And that signals is worth far more than a single ad. So today I'm going to show you the four-stage creative cycle that I used to take a concept from 100 per day static [music] image to dedicated landing page generating million of dollars in a single month. This is how you turn your winning ad idea into scalable long-term asset. Before I get into this framework, let me explain why most creative strategies fail. A typical approach looks like this. A media buyer tests a few concepts. One wins. They scale it. It works for a few weeks, then it starts to fatigue. Performance drops. They panic. They test new concept. Maybe one of those wins. They scale it. It fatigues again, and so on. This is a reactive strategy. You're always chasing the next winner, always one creative fatigue away from a performance crisis. Problem is not creative. The problem is the process. There's no systematic approach and development of a winning concept. There's no lifecycle. They're just test, win, fatigue, and repeat. The four-stage lifecycle I'm about to show you changes this. Instead of chasing winners, you're developing them. You're taking a concept has shown early promise and systematically investing in each stage, increasing your confidence and your budget as your evidence accumulates. Stage one is a static ad, the proof of concept. The purpose of a static ad is not to generate a revenue, unless you're selling a self-explanatory product. It's to validate whether the angle resonate with the audience at the lowest possible cost. Static ads are cheap to produce. A graphic designer can design a heaps of variation. Even AI can outdo that now. They're fast to launch. They provide a quick signal about whether the angle is worth investing in. The metrics we're looking at this stage are click-through rate and CPA. If both conditions are met after a week and 1K of spend, the concept advance to stage two. I want to be clear about what a static ad can and cannot tell. It can tell you whether the angle resonate, whether people are interested enough to click, but it cannot tell you whether the concept can scale. Static ads have ceiling. They fatigue quickly because they're primarily retargeting vehicle at a higher frequency. Then they cannot educate cold audience about the complex product, unless they're leading to advertorial or they're selling self-explanatory product. But as a proof of concept, as a cheap, fast way to validate the angle before investing in a video production, they're invaluable. One important warning is that if you're running a problem-solving like supplements, skin care, and your static ads are performing at a higher frequency, they're almost certainly doing retargeting, not prospecting. I've seen accounts where a static ad spent 10K at a frequency of three, while a video spent 100K with a frequency of 1.3. But the reality is the image was performing because video was generating top of the funnel that image was then doing middle of the funnel. The ROAS was inflated by the attribution overlap. So always check frequency when evaluating static ad performance. Above two probably means retargeting. Above three probably means saturation. If the static ad proves the concept, stage two is UGC. The purpose of UGC is to take validated angle and deliver it in a format that converts cold audience more effectively. Videos can educate, can build trust, and can create emotional connection in a static way cannot. The structure of a stage two test is same angle, same copy, same landing page, but delivered to multiple creators. Three to five creators usually delivering the same script in their own style. So why multiple creators? Because different creators resonate with a different audience segment. A 25-year-old female creator will resonate differently compared to 45-year-old male creator, even though they're delivering the same script. By testing multiple creators simultaneously, you identify which creator audience combination performs the best. Budget for this stage is between 200 and 500 per day, and duration is again 5 to 7 days. Your decision criteria is ROAS is above the target and the concept is outperforming the stage one static baseline by at least 20%. Advance to stage three. The improvements you should expect from stage one to two is significant. For a problem-solving product, it can typically improve your results by 20 to 50% over the static variation. And most importantly, it is doing prospecting. This is because video can do educational work that a static image cannot. Stage number three is influencer or whitelisted content. The purpose of stage three is to leverage the credibility and the social proof of an established creator. Your goal here is to reach new audience and improve conversion rate through whitelisting. It means running the ad through the creator handle, rather through your own brand account handle. So the ad appears that it's coming from a creator, not from a brand. This has two significant advantages. First, it access the creator audience, people who already trust and follow them. These are warm audience for the creators, even if they're cold audience for your brand. Conversion rate for this audience is typically higher because the trust transfer from the creator to your product is more powerful than a from a cold brand ad. Second, it provides social proof at a scale. When someone see an ad from a creator they follow, it carries implicit endorsement. If the person I trust is talking about this product, it must be worth considering. So imagine what happens when you have multiple creators like this, all talking about the same product. The budget for this stage is again 200 to 500 per day, but per creator. Again, decision criteria, if ROAS is above target and the concept is reaching new audience, where you can check by checking the frequency and checking percent of new visits, advance to stage four. So one important note on about stage three. Not every concept needs to go through the influencer content. For self-explanatory product with a strong visual appealing, UGC might be sufficient enough. Influencer content is most valuable for problem-solving product where the creator personally testifies and put his authority into vouching for this ad. Stage number four is dedicated landing page. This is where a winning concept becomes a long-term scalable asset. Purpose of a dedicated landing page is to maximize conversions by creating a fully congruent experience between the ad and the purchase decision. Instead of sending traffic to a generic landing page, you build a page specifically designed around the angle that has been proven to work. The structure of a dedicated landing page for a problem-solving product follows this sequence. Hook, where you open with the exact problem statement from the winning ad. Agitation, where you explain why the problem is worse than the customer thinks. Then social proof as with testimonial before and after results and review counts. And then the product benefits with the specific quantifiable outcomes. Offer with a price, guarantee, bonuses, and call to action. The improvement from a generic product page to a dedicated landing page is typically 30 to 50% if the angle is proven. The key principle for stage four is congruence. Everything on the page must match the angle in the ad. The headline must echo the hook. The social proof must validate the specific claim made in the ad. The offer must fulfill the promise made in the ad. Any breaking congruence reduces conversion rate. So let me put this as a practical timeline. Week number one, launch stage. One static concept per 100 or per day, three to five angles variation. Evaluate on Friday and Monday after you launch them on a Wednesday. Week number two, if the stage one validates the angle, take UGC with three to five creators. Stage number two starts with 200 to 500 per day. Identify the top performing creators. Reach out to an influencer in the same niche. Launch stage three is 500 to 2K per day. You have multiple creators that are performing. And if the concept is proven, brief a landing page designer on the angles. Build a dedicated landing page. What happens on an ongoing basis is that you're refreshing creatives weekly, test new creators delivering the same angle, also exploring the new angles with the statics. Monitor the frequency and monitor the fatigue. This is not four-week process. It's a four-stage investment process. You're increasing your investment in each stage as your confidence in the concept grows. You're not betting 10K on unproven concept. You're betting 500 to validate, then 2K to develop it, then 10K to scale it. So here's your takeaway. Your winning hook is not a destination. It's a starting point. >> [music] >> When you find an angle that resonates, when the static ads perform, when the click-through rate is strong, when the CPA is below the target, this is the beginning of the development process, not the end. Follow the four stages. Invest progressively. Build the evidence base before committing the budget. When the concept reaches stage four, when you have a proven angle, proven creative, and a dedicated landing page, you have an asset that can generate revenue for months. This is different between chasing winners and building winners. - An Antidote to Dissatisfaction: Kind: captions Language: en Everybody is familiar with the feeling that things are not as they should be. That you're not successful enough, your relationship's not satisfying enough, that you don't have the things you crave. A chronic dissatisfaction that makes you look outwards with envy and inwards with disappointment. Pop culture, advertising, and social media make this worse by reminding you that aiming for anything less than your dream job is failure, you need to have great experiences constantly, be conventionally attractive, have a lot of friends, and find your soulmate, and that others have all of these things and are truly happy. And, of course, a vast array of self-improvement products implies that it's all your fault for not working hard enough on yourself. In the last two decades, researchers have been starting to investigate how we can counteract these impulses. The field of positive psychology emerged, the study of what makes life worth living, while cognitive behavioral therapy was developed to change negative feelings. Scientists began to ask "Why are some people happier and more satisfied than others?" "And are there ways to apply what they're doing right to the rest of us?" In this video, we want to talk about one of the strongest predictors of how happy people are, how easily they make friends, and how good they are at dealing with hardship. An antidote to dissatisfaction, so to speak: Gratitude. While gratitude may sound like another self-improvement trend, preached by people who use hashtags, what we currently know about it is based on a body of scientific work and studies. We'll include them in the description. Gratitude can mean very different things to different people in different contexts. It's a character trait, a feeling, a virtue, and a behavior. You can feel grateful towards someone who did something for you, for random events, like the weather, or even for nature or fate, and it's wired into our biology. 1: How Gratitude Connects Us to Each Other. The predecessor of gratitude is probably reciprocity. It likely evolved as a biological signal that motivates animals to exchange things for their mutual benefit and can be found in the animal kingdom among certain fish, birds, or mammals, but especially in primates. When your brain recognizes that someone's done something nice for you, it reacts with gratitude to motivate you to repay them. This gratitude makes you care about others, and others care about you. This was important because, as human brains got better at reading emotions, selfish individuals were identified and shunned. It became an evolutionary advantage to play well with others and build lasting relationships. For example, if you were hungry and someone else showed you where to find tasty berries, you felt gratitude towards them and a bond to return the favor in the future, a drive to be pro-social. When you repaid them, they felt gratitude towards you. This brought your ancestors closer together and forged bonds and friendships. So, early forms of gratitude were biological mechanisms that modified your behavior towards cooperation, which helped humans to dominate Earth. But, over time, gratitude became more than just an impulse to play fair. 2: The Consequences of Gratitude Scientists found that gratitude stimulates the pathways in your brain involved in feelings of reward, forming social bonds, and interpreting other's intentions. It also makes it easier to save and retrieve positive memories Even more, gratitude directly counteracts negative feelings and traits, like envy and social comparison, narcissism, cynicism, and materialism. As a consequence, people who are grateful, no matter what for, tend to be happier and more satisfied. They have better relationships, an easier time making friends. They sleep better, tend to suffer less from depression, addiction, and burnout, and are better at dealing with traumatic events. In a way, gratitude makes it less likely that you'll fall into one of the psychological traps modern life has set for you. For example, gratitude measurably counters the tendency to forget and downplay positive events. If you work long and hard for something, actually getting it can feel daft and empty. You can find yourself emotionally back where you started and try to achieve the next biggest thing, looking for that satisfaction, instead of being satisfied with yourself. Or, imagine being lonely and wanting to have more friends. You actually might have someone or even multiple people who want to hang out, but you might feel that this is not enough, that you're a loser and feel bad about yourself. So you might turn down their attempts to hang out and become more lonely. If you feel grateful for your relationships instead, you might accept invitations or even take the initiative. The more often you risk opening up, the higher the chance of solidifying relationships and meeting new people. In the best case, gratitude can trigger a feedback loop. Positive feelings lead to more pro-social behavior, which leads to more positive social experiences that cause more positive feelings. This is a common experience after serious hardship, like chemotherapy, for example. Life can feel amazing after a crisis is over. The smallest things can be bottomless sources of joy, from being able to taste to just sitting in the sun or chatting with a friend. Objectively, your life is the same or maybe even slightly worse than before, but your brain compares your present experiences with the times when life was bad and reacts with gratitude. So, in a nutshell, gratitude refocuses your attention towards the good things you have, and the consequences of this shift are better feelings and more positive experiences. While it is great to know these things, is there actually a way for you to feel more of it? 3: How To Make Your Brain More Grateful The ability to experience more or less gratitude is not equally distributed. You have what's known as trait gratitude, that determines how much you are able to feel it. It depends on your genetics, personality, and culture. This discovery made scientists wonder if they could design exercises that change your trait gratitude and lead to more happiness. Let's start with important caveats. It's not yet entirely clear to what degree gratitude can be trained or how long the effects last. There are no magic pills for happiness. Life is complicated. On some days, it feels like you're in control of yourself, and, on others, you feel like you're not. And this is okay. Also, sometimes pursuing happiness can make you more unhappy if you put too much pressure on yourself. Gratitude should also not be seen as a solution to depression or a substitute for professional help,. It can only be a piece of the puzzle. It's not the solution to the puzzle itself. The easiest gratitude exercise, with the most solid research behind it, is gratitude journaling. It means sitting down for a few minutes, one to three times a week, and writing down five to ten things you're grateful for It might feel weird at first, so start simply. Can you feel grateful for a little thing? Like how great coffee is, or that someone was kind to you. Can you appreciate something someone else did for you? Can you reflect on which things or people you would miss if they were gone and be grateful that they're in your life? We're all different, so you'll know what works for you. And that's it, really. It feels almost insulting, like things shouldn't be that simple. But in numerous studies, the participants reported more happiness and a higher general life satisfaction after doing this practice for a few weeks. And, even more, studies have found changes in brain activity some months after they ended. Practicing gratitude may be a real way to reprogram yourself. This research shows that your emotions are not fixed. In the end, how you experience life is a representation of what you believe about it. If you attack your core beliefs about yourself and your life, you can change your thoughts and feelings, which automatically changes your behavior. It's pretty mind-blowing that something as simple as self-reflection can hack the pathways in our brain to fight dissatisfaction. And, if this is no reason to be more optimistic, what is? Being a human is hard, but it doesn't need to be as hard. And, if you actively look, you might find that your life is much better than you thought. [Happy bark] [Party horn] If you're curious and want to try out gratitude, we made a thing. Please note that you don't need to buy anything from anyone to practice gratitude. All you need is paper, a pen, and five minutes. Having said that, we've made a Kurzgesagt gratitude journal, based on studies we've read, conversations with experts, and our personal experiences with gratitude over the last year. It's structured in a way that might make it a bit easier to get into the habit of gratitude journaling. There are short explanations and reflections to mix it up and make it more interesting.   4. @bythelee: I have done some unique projects in my time. Many of them were "one off" builds. Get it wrong, there simply was no going back to do it over. One of those, was chopping off the back of my car, to convert a 4 door saloon with a trunk into a hatchback. I planned it for several years, until I finally felt I had "everything covered", and picked a day to make that first cut in the metal. Took many months, and ended up not quite the "perfect" end product, because I simply did not have access to the tools and materials needed for the "ultimate" job. But it was good enough, fulfilled the function, and did not stick out like an abomination. As I get older, I no longer have that time luxury. But I do still find that "letting it brew" pays dividends, and ALWAYS regret "just doing" prematurely.   However... this is NOT contradictory to the "iterate" suggestion!

I have ALSO come to realise, that my mind is able to "simulate" doing the job, and hence my process is similar to the advice here, to get started and iterate. 
I'm just doing that mentally, rather than physically. 
Saves on costs, saves on waste, is priceless when you only get one chance to do it, and I'm grateful that (so far) my skill to imagine the doing has not let me down. 
In other words, when I finally do get started, it all goes to plan, exactly as I had imagined it. No regrets, no wishing I hadn't started, no losing enthusiasm because it doesn't turn out like I wanted. 

The ultimate takeaway from this, is that getting a result you are satisfied with is going to take time. 
Whether simulating, practising, or iterating the actual job, you will learn from the process of moving the job forward, until you get to a time when that next iteration is "the ONE" where it all works well enough, to be satisfied with the outcome. I just tend to wait until I have thought it through enough times, to be confident I can make my ONE attempt be successful and acceptable. 


Also, if I doubt that I do have the practical skills to accomplish something (like, welding, brick laying, etc) I find small test projects to do where I can usefully practice and learn, WITHOUT ruining the single main project. 
For bricklaying (I wanted to build an extension on my house) I enrolled at my local college for a 3 month night course that taught me how to lay bricks properly. Rather than discover I was useless at it when trying to build my new front wall next to the road (where EVERYBODY could see how bad I was at it for perpetuity), I discovered that the tutor's guidance steered my novice skills into something I was quite happy with. I  practiced a little more, laying a small retaining wall in my back garden that supported a new patio, and it worked out magnificently (above expectation). That pushed my confidence high enough that I did not need to "iterate" to improve further, and felt ready to build the extension. 
It might have taken me between two and four times as long to lay every brick as a genuine craftsman, but, I got the extension built and it did NOT look like a DIY bodge job. 
Certainly not as perfect as if I had hired an experienced brickie to do it for me, but I was nevertheless proud of my work. (Which has stood the test of time, since that was 27 years ago.)

Small and quick tests and examples that exercise, practice, and improve the skills you might be doubting, is a GREAT way to build those skillsets without taking a lot of time or resources.

Whether you're planning your first booth or reworking an existing one, these insights will help you create a better, more effective exhibit experience. So, let's dive in. Number one, the first mistake we see is that people skip the budget conversation. It's important to have boundaries upfront when trying to get a new design for your booth. The result is you either get something too simple or something too ambitious that needs to be scaled back. When you're upfront about budget, your design partner can propose realistic solutions that look great and meet your goals. The second mistake we see is unclear or overloaded messaging. This simple transformation is what makes motion design powerful. So when you're thinking of concepts, do n't think of static visuals. Guess what the movement will do? Visual metaphor means representing an abstract idea through a simple visual. The human brain naturally understands symbols quickly. Therefore, when complex ideas are converted into simple visuals, communication becomes very effective. Let's see this with an example. An idea can be represented through a light bulb. Growth can be represented through a growing plant and connection can be represented through moving and connecting lines, like problem solving through fitting puzzle pieces. So, the more conversions you generate, the faster Meta is able to learn, because they have more data, and the shorter that learning phase will last, too. So, if you're working on a campaign that's generating thousands of sales a day, the learning phase can last hardly any time at all, because you really quickly have a lot of data. Meta's like, "Right, got it. Made the adjustments, new ads, understand it. We tested it. We worked out this is the way to go, and we're off." The smaller your budget, typically, the lower number of conversions you're going to generate, the longer it is going to take for you to exit the learning phase. So, if you are helicopter parenting your ad campaigns, you're constantly in there, constantly making tweaks and adjustments, you keep re-entering the learning phase, you're not allowing Meta time to optimize and get you the best performance possible. So, what I typically recommend advertisers do is try and set an optimization schedule. So, decide I'm going to adjust my campaigns no more than once every 7 days or 10 days. And you need to extend that time period because you are operating with a small budget and you are going to typically be generating lower conversion volumes. Now, you might set that schedule and realize that actually we could adjust more often this. We are getting good data within those time periods or you need to extend it and go the other way. That's going to depend on your business. Even within small budgets, if you're running an ad campaign that's designed to generate leads via a lead magnet, you're going to generate many, many more conversions than someone who's selling a high-ticket service well. So, again, you need to adjust the time frame accordingly. There is no one-size-fits-all when it comes time frame. One of the most common questions I get asked and I always say it's based on conversion volume is how often you should be making adjustments. It's not a we do it every 7 days across the board. Some campaigns generate thousands of conversions a day. Some campaigns generate six conversions a week. Well, the campaign that generates six conversions a week, it might take a month to know if a new ad is performing well, whereas the one that's generating thousands a day, it might take 3 hours. Like literally, I'm not over exaggerating that. That can absolutely be the case. So, you need to adjust the time frame according to conversion volume. One of the easiest ways if you're like, "Right, how do I know what's right for me?" is to use a statistical significance calculator. Free online tool, you enter in your numbers and the calculator will tell you, "Ad A is indeed outperforming Ad B with a 90% statistical significance, right?" It's a much better way to stand out, to niche down, and to to approach things that way. But with social media, it's post to post to post. You don't have to have an extremely high frequency. In fact, we found that this is key, that with growing frequency your Cost Per Click keeps growing as well. So you’re paying more for the second, third, fourth reach of a particular post. What is the ideal frequency? We went and found through our data and our massive ads benchmarking tools what is the ideal frequency. And the ideal frequency is simply one. Because you can do frequency capping, you can optimize to have one view. I would recommend to optimize a little over that, like not near two, and cut the ads at 1.2 or 1.3 frequency. Find the ideal frequency for your message. Post a little less than you might have had to. But make sure you get the right message to the right people. And Relevance Score and frequency are perfect metrics to always watch. Thank you. I'm Jan Rezab, Watch us next week. Every Monday morning.

Cost per acquisition or your CPA is king. The first thing that you need to do is you need to determine how much you can spend on your ads to profitably acquire a new customer. And to do that, the formula is quite simple. So to find your break even CPA, you take the average order value on your store and you multiply that by the gross margin. So, let's say that every time a customer buys from your store, on average, you get $60 in revenue. And let's say that your gross margin is 60%. So, basically, 40% of that $60 you have to spend on fulfilling the product. Then, all you have to do is take the $60, multiply it by 60%, and you find out that your break even CPA is $36. Now, the rule of thumb here is if your CPA is below break even, so you're profitable, then you want to scale carefully. If your CPA is 10 to 20% above break even, so maybe it's costing you $40 to get a purchase, then you're in the optimization window. If your CPA is way above break even and you're just not acquiring customers or customers are costing you hundreds of dollars in spend, then kill the campaign. Another key metric you should be looking at is the 3second view rate. So generally on Facebook, you want to look for 30% or more. That's quite strong and it shows you that people are really engaging with your ads and the content you've created is interesting. If it's 20 to 30% workable, but it could probably use some more optimization or changes. And if it's below 20%, that's a good indication that it's a bad ad. Next, you have CTR or click-through rate. So, this is the percentage of people that see your ad and then decide to click on it and go to your website. Generally, looking at 1.5% and above is quite healthy. If you're below that or under 1%, then you should definitely optimize or start making new ads. It's likely that you have a bad angle or a weak offer. Another metric to keep in mind is your CPC or your cost per click. So, if the CTR is high, meaning that tons of people are clicking on your ad, but the cost per click is also high, then maybe it's a targeting mismatch and your ads are just going to the wrong people or you're in a super competitive market and you should probably switch the marketing angle and try to find a new customer avatar. If the CTR is very low and the CPC is also high, then that just tells you it's a bad creative and it's costing you a ton of money to drive any kind of clicks. Now, I could go on and on about all the different metrics that you could read, but remember, CPA is king, and you want to make sure your creative is good by looking at the 3-se secondond view rate as well as the CTR and how the CTR compares with the CPC. That's a video trend, but I think how can I apply that to my images? Well, I could do a carousel with two different images where the first one is the before state and then you swipe across, and the second image shows the after state. Here's a quick example for you. Let's think about if you're somebody who teaches how to get organized, you could show a before state image of a messy office, things everywhere, and then they swipe left and look at the second image in the carousel, and the office is tidy and perfectly organized. That is how you could take that video trend, adapt it to images, and then use it on Facebook and Instagram. So the key here is to spend time on other platforms, find trends, see what's working to your Facebook and Instagram ads. Now, the next one, we touched on this earlier is to use native formats. For Facebook and Instagram, I recommend using square images or the portrait type which is, I think it's 1080 by 1350 on Instagram, because that tends to be what people are starting to use organically now. So make sure when you're creating ads, follow these tips that I gave you earlier, and when you do it, use these organic native looking formats so that you don't instantly get filtered out no matter what you do as being an ad simply because of the format that you used.
